verses.text: But false prophets also arose among the people, as false teachers will also be among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, denying even the Master who bought them, bringing on themselves swift destruction.
Many will follow their immoral  ways, and as a result, the way of the truth will be maligned.
In covetousness they will exploit you with deceptive words: whose sentence now from of old doesn’t linger, and their destruction will not slumber.
For if God didn’t spare angels when they sinned, but cast them down to Tartarus,  and committed them to pits of darkness, to be reserved for judgment;
and didn’t spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah with seven others, a preacher of righteousness, when he brought a flood on the world of the ungodly;
and turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah into ashes, condemned them to destruction, having made them an example to those who would live ungodly;
and delivered righteous Lot, who was very distressed by the lustful life of the wicked
(for that righteous man dwelling among them, was tormented in his righteous soul from day to day with seeing and hearing lawless deeds):
the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation and to keep the unrighteous under punishment for the day of judgment;
but chiefly those who walk after the flesh in the lust of defilement, and despise authority. Daring, self-willed, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignitaries;
whereas angels, though greater in might and power, don’t bring a railing judgment against them before the Lord.
But these, as unreasoning creatures, born natural animals to be taken and destroyed, speaking evil in matters about which they are ignorant, will in their destroying surely be destroyed,
receiving the wages of unrighteousness; people who count it pleasure to revel in the daytime, spots and defects, reveling in their deceit while they feast with you;
having eyes full of adultery, and who can’t cease from sin; enticing unsettled souls; having a heart trained in greed; children of cursing;
forsaking the right way, they went astray, having followed the way of Balaam the son of Beor, who loved the wages of wrongdoing;
but he was rebuked for his own disobedience. A mute donkey spoke with a man’s voice and stopped the madness of the prophet.
These are wells without water, clouds driven by a storm; for whom the blackness of darkness has been reserved forever.
For, uttering great swelling words of emptiness, they entice in the lusts of the flesh, by licentiousness, those who are indeed escaping from those who live in error;
promising them liberty, while they themselves are bondservants of corruption; for a man is brought into bondage by whoever overcomes him.

For if, after they have escaped the defilement of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in it and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first.
For it would be better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.
But it has happened to them according to the true proverb, “The dog turns to his own vomit again,”  and “the sow that has washed to wallowing in the mire.”

footnotes.content: Peter warns that deception doesn't come from outside the faith—false teachers rise within the very community, in sheep's clothing. They distort Christ Himself, denying His lordship while bearing His name. What a quiet danger: trusting voices that wear the mask of faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sad part is not just that they deceive—it's that their slander reaches the ears of the watching world. When those who claim Christ live contrary to His way, unbelievers see and say, "So this is what that faith produces." Our lives write the truth or lie.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even ancient warnings show a pattern: the false make their living by smooth talk and exploitation. Peter says their sentence isn't delayed—judgment is already at work. God does not sleep; He sees every greedy hand and empty promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter begins his proof: even the angels who fell—beings of tremendous power—could not escape God's judgment. He cast them to Tartarus, the deep pit. If power itself offers no refuge from the Lord's hand, neither will pride or eloquence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Noah preached righteousness for 120 years while building the ark, yet the world mocked and went its way. Then God brought the flood—not sudden, but inevitable. The Lord preserved Noah and his household. Faithful witness and patience precede salvation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sodom and Gomorrah became ash—not erased from history, but made an example, a warning carved into memory. Peter shows that God judges the openly wicked, that the cost of ungodly living is visible and unmistakable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lot was righteous, yet he dwelt among the wicked. He was "greatly distressed"—worn down by their ways, burdened by the godlessness around him. Righteousness is not immunity from sorrow; it is sorrow seen clearly and borne faithfully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Day after day, Lot's righteous soul was tormented—watching, listening to the lawlessness of Sodom. He could not unhear what he heard, could not unsee what he saw. Sometimes faithfulness means living with a broken heart in an unbroken world.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is the heart of it: the Lord *knows* how to deliver His own from temptation and trial, and simultaneously knows how to keep the unrighteous reserved for their day. His knowledge is not merely knowing—it is active wisdom, delivering and preserving according to His purposes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter describes the false teachers: they follow flesh and lust, despise authority, dare to mock what they should reverence. Self-will masquerades as freedom; coarseness parades as boldness. They've lost the fear of the Lord, and it shows in their contempt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even angels—vastly stronger, of greater power—do not bring railing judgment against these people before the Lord. The implication stings: these self-willed teachers speak evil of those they should reverence, showing less restraint than beings of immense might.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They are like unreasoning animals, natural creatures made for capture and destruction. They speak with authority on matters they're ignorant of. Their very ignorance becomes their snare—they're headed for the ruin they mock.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They feast with you, yet they are stains and blemishes—their delight is in revelry, their reward is unrighteousness. What a picture: reclining at table alongside the faithful, all the while counting pleasure what Christ calls sin. They mock by their very presence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their eyes are full of adultery—always looking, always lusting, never satisfied. They've trained their hearts in greed from youth. Peter calls them "children of cursing"—born into patterns of disobedience, shaped by appetite, destined for judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Balaam, the son of Beor, loved the wages of wrongdoing—he would prophesy for pay, selling his gift for gold. Peter names him as the pattern: those who abandon the right way to follow greed repeat the ancient sin of mercenary faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But God rebuked him—a mute donkey spoke with a human voice and halted the prophet's madness. The animal's rebuke was literal, unstoppable. Even creation obeys God's will to correct those who refuse His voice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wells without water, clouds driven by storm—they promise refreshment but offer only emptiness. They promise light but scatter only shadow. For such as these, "the blackness of darkness" is reserved forever—separation from all truth, all goodness, all home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice the target: those barely escaping error are most vulnerable. People tasting freedom for the first time, newly turning from their old paths—these are seduced by grand-sounding, empty words and promises of liberty. Timely mercy often precedes a new temptation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They promise freedom while enslaved themselves—servants of corruption. A profound irony: those who claim to lead others to liberty are chained to their own appetites. The one who overcomes you makes you his bondservant; the false teachers have already been conquered by their lusts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Worse than before: those who escaped the world's defilement through knowing Christ, then turned back and were entangled again—their last state is worse than their first. Knowledge rejected hardens the heart in ways ignorance never could.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Better never to have tasted the way of righteousness than to taste it and turn back. The holy commandment has been "delivered to them"—it was not hidden, not unclear. To reject it after knowing it is to choose darkness with open eyes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo: a dog returning to its vomit, a washed sow rolling in mire. We see it again and again—people who turn from Christ only to return to their old patterns, dragging mud back into a house they'd left. The proverb is ancient but its warning remains present.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
